Hebbian principles, experiments with Aplysia, and long-term potentiation provide ways to investigate the cellular mechanisms involved."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The module traces how changes at synapses might support lasting behavior change. Keep experimental findings about specific cells and circuits distinct from broad claims about improving everyday memory."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-3-study-1","text":"Learning changes synaptic relationships"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At the cellular level, a memory requires some lasting effect of experience on neural signaling. The Hebbian principle captures a basic possibility: connections between neurons can become more effective when their activities are repeatedly associated. The details are more complex than a slogan, but the principle provides a bridge from learning in behavior to changing strength in a circuit. Experiments can test this idea by measuring how a synapse responds before and after patterns of stimulation."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-3-study-2","text":"Why Aplysia is instructive"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Studies of the sea slug Aplysia helped link observable learning to identifiable changes in neural transmission. Habituation describes a reduced response after repeated harmless stimulation; sensitization describes an enhanced response following certain salient events. These patterns involve changes in synaptic processes and can differ in their duration. The value of this model is not that humans learn exactly like a sea slug but that relatively simple circuits allow investigation of mechanisms difficult to isolate in larger brains."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-3-study-3","text":"Long-term potentiation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Long-term potentiation (LTP) describes a persistent increase in synaptic effectiveness following appropriate stimulation. In many well-studied cases, changes involve glutamate receptors, calcium-related signaling, and alterations in postsynaptic response. Different forms of synaptic plasticity have different requirements and time courses. LTP is an important candidate mechanism for some kinds of learning, but it should not be described as identical to a complete autobiographical memory."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-3-study-4","text":"Limits of memory enhancement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Improving memory can involve practice, retrieval, spacing, sleep, and other behavioral conditions as well as biological processes. Claims about a universal memory-enhancing substance or simple brain intervention require evidence. Effective studying is more than exposing the brain to information once: durable change depends on repeated engagement and appropriate retrieval. Link cellular processes to behavioral learning without assuming that a single synapse explains an entire skill or recollection."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h01","text":"Blind Alleys and Abandoned Mines"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Textbooks, including this one, concentrate mostly on successful research that led to our current understanding of a field.","sourcePrintedPage":407,"sourcePdfPage":425,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It explores one direction after another, a little like a rat in a complex maze, abandoning the dead ends and pursuing arms that lead further.","sourcePrintedPage":407,"sourcePdfPage":425,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The problem with the maze analogy is that an investigator seldom runs into a wall that clearly identifies the end of a route.","sourcePrintedPage":407,"sourcePdfPage":425,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A better analogy is a prospector digging for gold, never certain whether to abandon an unprofitable spot or to keep digging just a little longer.","sourcePrintedPage":407,"sourcePdfPage":425,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many previously exciting lines of research in the study of learning are now of little more than historical interest.","sourcePrintedPage":407,"sourcePdfPage":425,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h02","text":"Learning and the Hebbian Synapse"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Research on the physiology of learning began with Ivan Pavlov’s concept of classical conditioning.","sourcePrintedPage":408,"sourcePdfPage":426,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hebb suggested that when the axon of neuron A “repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing [neuron B], some growth process or metabolic change takes place in one or both cells” that increases the subsequent ability of axon A to excite cell B .","sourcePrintedPage":408,"sourcePdfPage":426,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In other words, an axon that has been paired with strong depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron becomes more successful in the future.","sourcePrintedPage":408,"sourcePdfPage":426,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In still simpler words, “cells that fire together wire together.” Later researchers slightly modified this idea: Neurons that are near each other and fire together wire together .","sourcePrintedPage":408,"sourcePdfPage":426,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That saying is less catchy, but it acknowledges that the structure of the nervous system determines which connections are possible.","sourcePrintedPage":408,"sourcePdfPage":426,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Pairing activity in axons A and C increases the future effect of A on B.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A Hebbian synapse is one that increases its effectiveness because of simultaneous activity in the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h03","text":"Single-Cell Mechanisms of Invertebrate Behavior Change"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If you want to look for a needle in a haystack, a good strategy is to look in a small haystack.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many researchers have turned to studies of invertebrates.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems are organized differently, but the chemistry of the neuron, the principles of the action potential, the neurotransmitters, and their receptors are the same.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If we identify the physical basis of learning and memory in an invertebrate, we have at least a hypothesis of what might work in vertebrates.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Biologists have long used this strategy for studying genetics, embryology, and other biological processes.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h04","text":"Aplysia as an Experimental Animal"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Aplysia , a marine invertebrate related to slugs, has been a popular animal for studies of the physiology of learning (Figure 12.15).","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Compared to vertebrates, it has fewer neurons, many of which are large and easy to study.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike vertebrates, Aplysia neurons are virtually identical from one individual to another so that investigators can replicate one another’s work in detail.","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Much research deals with the withdrawal response: Any touch to the siphon, mantle, or gill of an Aplysia (Figure 12.16) evokes a withdrawal response of the irritated","sourcePrintedPage":409,"sourcePdfPage":427,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Investigators have traced the neural path from the touch receptors through other neurons to the motor neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h05","text":"Habituation in Aplysia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is accompanied by no change in other stimuli.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If we repeatedly stimulate an Aplysia ’s gills with a brief jet of seawater, it withdraws at first, but after many repetitions, it stops responding.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The decline in response is not due to muscle fatigue; even after habituation has occurred, direct stimulation of the motor neuron produces a full-size muscle contraction .","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The response in the sensory neuron is the same as before, but it produces less excitation in the motor neuron .","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We are therefore left with the conclusion that habituation in Aplysia depends on a change in a synapse between the sensory neuron and the motor neuron (Figure 12.17).","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h06","text":"Sensitization in Aplysia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This phenomenon is sensitization , an increase in response to mild stimuli, caused by exposure to more intense stimuli.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Similarly, a strong stimulus almost anywhere on Aplysia ’s skin intensifies a later withdrawal response to a touch.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers traced sensitization to changes at identified synapses (Cleary et al., 1989; Dale et al., 1988; Kandel","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Strong stimulation on the skin excites a facilitating interneuron that releases serotonin onto the presynaptic terminals of many sensory neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because potassium now flows more slowly out of the cell, the membrane repolarizes more slowly after an action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Repeating this process causes the sensory neuron to synthesize new proteins that produce long-term sensitization .","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h07","text":"Long-Term Potentiation in Vertebrates"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Neuroscientists have long assumed that learning depends on changes at synapses, and the work on Aplysia supports that idea.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The first evidence for a similar process among vertebrates came from studies of neurons in the rat hippocampus .","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The phenomenon, known as long-term potentiation (LTP) , is this: One or more axons connected to a dendrite bombard it with a rapid series of stimuli.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The burst of intense stimulation leaves some of the synapses potentiated (more responsive to new input) for minutes, days, or weeks.","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Long-term depression (LTD) , a prolonged decrease in response at a synapse, occurs for axons that have been less active than others, such as axon 3 in Figure 12.17","sourcePrintedPage":411,"sourcePdfPage":429,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h08","text":"Biochemical Mechanisms"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Determining how LTP or LTD occurs has been a huge research challenge because each neuron has many tiny synapses, sometimes in the tens of thousands.","sourcePrintedPage":411,"sourcePdfPage":429,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Isolating the chemical changes at any synapse takes an enormous amount of creative, patient research.","sourcePrintedPage":411,"sourcePdfPage":429,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"LTP occurs most readily in the hippocampus, and its mechanisms have been most extensively studied there.","sourcePrintedPage":411,"sourcePdfPage":429,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Here we are interested in two types of glutamate receptors, called AMPA and NMDA.","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The AMPA receptor is excited by the neurotransmitter glutamate, but it can also respond to a drug called a -amino- 3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (mercifully abbreviated AMPA).","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The NMDA receptor’s response depends on the degree of polarization across the membrane.","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because a CaMKII remains at the stimulated synapse and does not diffuse elsewhere, it is responsible for the specificity aspect of LTP—the fact that only the activated synapses become strengthened .","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The formation and maintenance of LTP depends on all these chemicals— a CaMKII, CREB, and BDNF .","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In other cases, it builds new dendrites and synapses that form a functional cluster with the dendrites already present .","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Let’s summarize: When glutamate massively stimulates AMPA receptors, the resulting depolarization enables glutamate to stimulate nearby NMDA receptors also.","sourcePrintedPage":412,"sourcePdfPage":430,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Research on LTP shows us a mechanism whereby experience can alter the input– output properties of a neuron.","sourcePrintedPage":413,"sourcePdfPage":431,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, it should be clear that understanding LTP is just one step toward understanding learning.","sourcePrintedPage":413,"sourcePdfPage":431,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-3-h09","text":"Improving Memory"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers study the biological mechanisms of memory for theoretical reasons but also in the hope of practical applications.","sourcePrintedPage":413,"sourcePdfPage":431,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"marketed so far to improve memory act as stimulants or by improving .","sourcePrintedPage":414,"sourcePdfPage":432,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most of the research on G. biloba has been of low quality, and the results have .","sourcePrintedPage":414,"sourcePdfPage":432,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Several companies market over-the-counter supplements that claim to help brain The Hebbian principle captures a basic possibility: connections between neurons can become more effective when their activities are repeatedly associated. The details are more complex than a slogan, but the principle provides a bridge from learning in behavior to changing strength in a circuit. Habituation describes a reduced response after repeated harmless stimulation; sensitization describes an enhanced response following certain salient events. These patterns involve changes in synaptic processes and can differ in their duration. The value of this model is not that humans learn exactly like a sea slug but that relatively simple circuits allow investigation of mechanisms difficult to isolate in larger brains.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":407,"sourcePrintedEnd":416,"sourcePdfStart":425,"sourcePdfEnd":434},{"id":"bp14-m12-3-study-3","title":"Long-term potentiation","text":"Long-term potentiation (LTP) describes a persistent increase in synaptic effectiveness following appropriate stimulation. LTP is an important candidate mechanism for some kinds of learning, but it should not be described as identical to a complete autobiographical memory.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":407,"sourcePrintedEnd":416,"sourcePdfStart":425,"sourcePdfEnd":434},{"id":"bp14-m12-3-study-4","title":"Limits of memory enhancement","text":"Improving memory can involve practice, retrieval, spacing, sleep, and other behavioral conditions as well as biological processes. Effective studying is more than exposing the brain to information once: durable change depends on repeated engagement and appropriate retrieval. .","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":18},{"text":"In other words, an axon that has been paired with strong depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron becomes more successful in the future.","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":19},{"text":"In still simpler words, “cells that fire together wire .","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":20},{"text":"That saying is less catchy, but it acknowledges that the structure of the nervous system determines which connections are possible.","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":21},{"text":"Pairing activity in axons A and C increases the future effect of A on B.","printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":22},{"text":"A Hebbian synapse is one that increases its effectiveness because of simultaneous activity in the presynaptic and postsynaptic .","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":39},{"text":"The response in the sensory neuron is the same as before, but it and the Hebbian Synapse","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"facts":[{"text":"Research on the physiology of learning began with Ivan Pavlov’s concept of classical conditioning.","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":17},{"text":"Hebb suggested that when the axon of neuron A “repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing [neuron B], some growth process or metabolic change takes place in one or both cells” that increases the subsequent ability of axon A to excite cell B .","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":18},{"text":"In other words, an axon that has been paired with strong depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron becomes more successful in the future.","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":19},{"text":"In still simpler words, “cells that fire together wire together.” Later researchers slightly modified this idea: Neurons that are near each other and fire together wire together .","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":20},{"text":"That saying is less catchy, but it acknowledges that the structure of the nervous system determines which connections are possible.","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":21},{"text":"Pairing activity in axons A and C increases the future effect of A on B.","printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":22},{"text":"A Hebbian synapse is one that increases its effectiveness because of simultaneous activity in the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons.","printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":23},{"text":"Although that theory led Karl Lashley to an unsuccessful search for connections in the cerebral cortex, it also stimulated Donald Hebb to propose a mechanism for change at a synapse.","printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":85}],"originalFacts":7,"additionalFacts":1,"glossary":[{"term":"Hebbian vertebrates, it has fewer neurons, many of which are large and easy to detail.","printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":33},{"text":"Much research deals with the withdrawal response: Any touch to the siphon, mantle, or gill of an Aplysia (Figure 12.16) evokes a withdrawal response of the irritated","printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":34},{"text":"Investigators have traced the neural path from the touch receptors through other neurons to the motor neurons.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":35},{"text":"Using this neural pathway, investigators have studied learned changes in behavior.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":86},{"text":"In 2000, Eric Kandel won a Nobel Prize for this work.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":87}],"originalFacts":5,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[{"term":"Motor neuron","definition":"neuron that receives excitation from other neurons and conducts impulses to a muscle","sourcePrintedPage":627,"sourcePdfPage":645},{"term":"Withdrawal","definition":"effects of drug cessation","sourcePrintedPage":635,"sourcePdfPage":653}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":127,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":126},{"id":"bp14-m12-3-h05","title":"Habituation in Aplysia","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m12-3-h03","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"facts":[{"text":"Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is accompanied by no change in other stimuli.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":37},{"text":"If we repeatedly stimulate an Aplysia ’s gills with a brief jet of seawater, it withdraws at first, but after many repetitions, it stops responding.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":38},{"text":"The decline in response is not due to muscle fatigue; even after habituation has occurred, direct stimulation of the motor neuron produces a full-size muscle contraction .","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":39},{"text":"The response in the sensory neuron is the same as before, but it produces less excitation in the motor neuron .","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":40},{"text":"We are therefore left with the conclusion that habituation in Aplysia depends on a change in a synapse between the sensory neuron and the motor neuron (Figure 12.17).","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":41},{"text":"For example, a sudden noise may startle you, but you respond less after repeated presentations.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":88},{"text":"We can also rule out changes in the sensory neuron.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":89}],"originalFacts":5,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[{"term":"Habituation","definition":"a more intense stimuli.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":43},{"text":"Similarly, a strong stimulus almost anywhere on stimulation on the skin excites a facilitating interneuron that releases serotonin onto the presynaptic terminals of many sensory neurons.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Because potassium now flows more slowly out of the cell, the membrane repolarizes more slowly after an action potential.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":47},{"text":"Repeating this process causes the sensory neuron to synthesize new proteins that produce long-term sensitization .","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":48},{"text":"If you experience an unexpected sharp pain, you temporarily react more strongly than usual to other sudden stimuli.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":90},{"text":"Therefore, the presynaptic neuron continues releasing its neurotransmitter for longer than usual.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":91},{"text":"This research shows how it is possible to explain one example of behavioral plasticity in terms of molecular events.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":92},{"text":"Other studies explored mechanisms of classical and instrumental conditioning in .","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":51},{"text":"The phenomenon, known as long-term potentiation (LTP) , is this: One or more axons connected to a dendrite bombard it with a rapid series of stimuli.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"The burst of intense stimulation leaves some of the synapses weeks.","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"Long-term depression (LTD) , a prolonged decrease in response at a synapse, occurs for axons that have been less active than others, such as axon 3 in Figure 12.17","printedPage":411,"pdfPage":429,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"If learning produced only a strengthening of synapses, then every time you learned something, your brain would get more and more active, constantly burning more and more fuel.","printedPage":411,"pdfPage":429,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":94}],"originalFacts":5,"additionalFacts":1,"glossary":[{"term":"Long-term .","printedPage":412,"pdfPage":430,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":62},{"text":"The formation and maintenance of LTP depends on all these chemicals— .","printedPage":412,"pdfPage":430,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"Let’s summarize: When glutamate massively stimulates AMPA receptors, the resulting depolarization enables glutamate to stimulate nearby NMDA receptors also.","printedPage":412,"pdfPage":430,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":65},{"text":"Research on LTP shows us a mechanism whereby experience can clear that understanding LTP is just one step toward understanding learning.","printedPage":413,"pdfPage":431,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":67},{"text":"AMPA and NMDA Synapses In some cases, LTP occurs at GABA A mechanism needs direct supporting evidence, not only a metaphor.","paragraphIndex":20000,"bullets":[{"label":"Competing explanations","explanation":"A neural circuit can change its response through modified connections, intrinsic excitability or other processes; an account should specify which change predicts behavior.","paragraphIndex":20001},{"label":"Scientific correction","explanation":"When studies contradict a simple localization or chemical-memory claim, researchers refine the hypothesis rather than assume any single finding settles every form of learning.","paragraphIndex":20002},{"label":"From speculation to mechanism","explanation":"Broad claims about a 'memory molecule' or a unique storage site need experiments that isolate a specific learning process.","paragraphIndex":74300},{"label":"Evaluate a mechanism","explanation":"Ask whether the manipulation changes learning, retrieval, performance, or all three; distinguish a plausible correlate from a demonstrated mechanism.","paragraphIndex":74301}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Memory research contains many once-attractive ideas that proved inadequate when tested. A good biological account must explain why a memory changes behavior, which cells are altered, and whether the proposed change is necessary.","followUpParagraphIndex":53200,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h02","title":"Learning and the Hebbian Synapse","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":408,"pdfPage":426,"explanation":"The Hebbian principle proposes that correlated activity can strengthen the effectiveness of a synapse. It is a framework for explaining how experience leaves a change in a neural network.","paragraphIndex":20003,"bullets":[{"label":"Coincidence","explanation":"If a presynaptic input repeatedly contributes to postsynaptic firing, the connection may become more effective.","paragraphIndex":20004},{"label":"Boundary","explanation":"“Cells that fire together wire together” is a shorthand, not a universal rule; the timing, type of synapse and local biochemical conditions matter.","paragraphIndex":20005},{"label":"Coincident activity","explanation":"Timing and patterns of activity can make a synapse more effective, creating a possible cellular basis for learning an association.","paragraphIndex":74302},{"label":"Meaning and limit","explanation":"'Cells that fire together wire together' is a useful shorthand, not a complete law governing all plasticity. Synapses can also weaken, and different circuits use different rules.","paragraphIndex":74303}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Hebb proposed that connections strengthen when the sending neuron repeatedly helps activate the receiving neuron. This became a central framework for studying experience-dependent synaptic change.","followUpParagraphIndex":53201,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h03","title":"Single-Cell Mechanisms of Invertebrate Behavior Change","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"explanation":"Studying a simple invertebrate circuit makes it possible to link an elementary behavioral change to identifiable neurons. The goal is not to claim that all human memory works like one reflex.","paragraphIndex":20006,"bullets":[{"label":"Reduction","explanation":"A small nervous system permits careful observation of which cells change during habituation, sensitization or conditioning.","paragraphIndex":20007},{"label":"General value","explanation":"The experiment demonstrates that a behavioral change can arise from specific, experimentally testable synaptic processes.","paragraphIndex":20008},{"label":"Why invertebrates","explanation":"Some species have large, identifiable neurons and comparatively accessible circuits.","paragraphIndex":74304},{"label":"What counts as learning","explanation":"A change in response after repeated stimulation must be distinguished from fatigue, damage, or changes in the muscles used to perform the response.","paragraphIndex":74305}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Simple nervous systems allow researchers to link defined cells and synapses to changes in behavior. The experimental advantage is that the pathway producing a response can be traced more directly.","followUpParagraphIndex":53202,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h04","title":"Aplysia as an Experimental Animal","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m12-3-h03","printedPage":409,"pdfPage":427,"explanation":"The marine mollusk Aplysia has unusually large and accessible nerve cells. Researchers used its withdrawal responses as a model for elementary learning.","paragraphIndex":20009,"bullets":[{"label":"Why this organism","explanation":"Identifiable neurons and simple reflex pathways allow investigators to connect stimulus, synaptic response and change in behavior.","paragraphIndex":20010},{"label":"Limits of the analogy","explanation":"A simple reflex cannot represent all the components of autobiographical memory, but it can reveal the molecular logic of plasticity.","paragraphIndex":20011},{"label":"Preparation","explanation":"Researchers can repeatedly stimulate the siphon or other body parts and record how a withdrawal response changes.","paragraphIndex":74306},{"label":"Scientific value","explanation":"The task is not a model of every human memory, but it provides clear examples of how short- and long-lasting changes in synaptic functioning can affect behavior.","paragraphIndex":74307}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"The marine mollusk Aplysia has been studied because its defensive withdrawal responses can be observed while scientists examine the neurons contributing to them.","followUpParagraphIndex":53203,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"concise_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h05","title":"Habituation in Aplysia","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m12-3-h03","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"explanation":"Habituation is a reduction in response to a harmless stimulus that occurs repeatedly. It is a form of learning rather than merely sensory damage or tired muscles when it can be traced to altered transmission.","paragraphIndex":20012,"bullets":[{"label":"Synaptic change","explanation":"In the Aplysia withdrawal circuit, repeated mild stimulation can reduce transmitter release at relevant sensory-neuron terminals.","paragraphIndex":20013},{"label":"Behavioral interpretation","explanation":"The animal becomes less responsive to a familiar, inconsequential touch, conserving response for more important events.","paragraphIndex":20014},{"label":"Behavioral pattern","explanation":"Repeated gentle stimulation leads to a smaller withdrawal response in Aplysia under appropriate conditions.","paragraphIndex":74308},{"label":"Cellular account","explanation":"Reduced transmitter release at relevant sensory-to-motor connections contributes to the response decline. It differs from losing the ability to respond to a novel or stronger stimulus.","paragraphIndex":74309}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Habituation is a decline in response after repeated presentation of a harmless stimulus. It can be understood as learning that the repeatedly occurring event need not produce a strong response.","followUpParagraphIndex":53204,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"concise_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h06","title":"Sensitization in Aplysia","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m12-3-h03","printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"explanation":"Sensitization is increased responsiveness after a strong or important stimulus. In Aplysia, the process shows how one pathway can modulate another.","paragraphIndex":20015,"bullets":[{"label":"Facilitatory signal","explanation":"A strong stimulus activates interneurons that release serotonin onto sensory-neuron terminals, changing ion-channel activity and strengthening transmitter release.","paragraphIndex":20016},{"label":"Longer effect","explanation":"Repeated sensitizing experiences can recruit protein synthesis and more durable cellular changes; the duration of learning reflects different biological processes.","paragraphIndex":20017},{"label":"Behavioral effect","explanation":"After an aversive stimulus, a previously weak touch can evoke a stronger defensive response.","paragraphIndex":74310},{"label":"Synaptic process","explanation":"Modulatory neurons and intracellular chemical changes increase the efficacy of relevant synapses. Longer-lasting effects can require protein synthesis and changes in synaptic structure.","paragraphIndex":74311}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Sensitization increases responsiveness following a strong or disturbing event. It differs from habituation because the system becomes more reactive rather than less reactive.","followUpParagraphIndex":53205,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"concise_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h07","title":"Long-Term Potentiation in Vertebrates","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":410,"pdfPage":428,"explanation":"Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a persistent increase in synaptic effectiveness after certain patterns of stimulation. It has been studied extensively in hippocampal circuits.","paragraphIndex":20018,"bullets":[{"label":"Basic observation","explanation":"Following strong or coordinated activity, later input can produce a larger postsynaptic response at the same synapses.","paragraphIndex":20019},{"label":"Interpretation","explanation":"LTP is an experimentally tractable model of synaptic plasticity, not proof that every individual memory is simply LTP at a single connection.","paragraphIndex":20020},{"label":"Induction","explanation":"Repeated or coordinated activity can strengthen communication between connected cells, often involving glutamate receptors and postsynaptic calcium signaling.","paragraphIndex":74312},{"label":"Evidence and caution","explanation":"LTP shares mechanisms with some kinds of learning, but it is not identical to every memory. Researchers must test how changes in a synapse relate to behavior.","paragraphIndex":74313}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a persistent increase in the strength of a synapse following certain patterns of activity. It is a major experimental model for studying synaptic plasticity in vertebrates.","followUpParagraphIndex":53206,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","masterclass":{"id":"bp14-m12-3-h07","points":[{"label":"Activity-dependent induction","explanation":"In many preparations, an appropriate pattern of presynaptic and postsynaptic activity leads to a persistent increase in the response produced by later stimulation of the same synapse.","paragraphIndex":730361},{"label":"NMDA and calcium","explanation":"Some hippocampal forms of LTP depend on conditions that permit NMDA-type glutamate receptors to pass calcium. Intracellular signaling then changes how the synapse responds.","paragraphIndex":730362},{"label":"Expression and persistence","explanation":"Changes can include the activity or number of postsynaptic receptors and, over longer periods, alterations that require additional protein synthesis or structural change.","paragraphIndex":730363},{"label":"Behavioral interpretation","explanation":"A plasticity mechanism can contribute to learning without being a complete explanation of remembering a person's life. The question is whether changes are necessary for the relevant behavior and under what conditions.","paragraphIndex":730364}],"explanation":"Long-term potentiation (LTP) is an experimental example of experience-dependent strengthening of synaptic transmission. It offers a plausible cellular mechanism for some forms of memory, although the relationship between LTP and complete human memories is complex.","caution":"LTP does not mean every time someone learns, all of the brain's synapses permanently become stronger; weakening and regulation also occur.","checkQuestion":"Why does activity at a synapse need to be linked with the postsynaptic cell's state for an associative plasticity rule to work?","title":"Long-Term Potentiation in Vertebrates","sourcePrintedPage":410,"sourcePdfPage":428,"explanationIndex":730360,"cautionIndex":730405,"questionIndex":730406,"kind":"original_classroom_walkthrough","editorialStatus":"individually_written_source_grounded_explanation","depth":"extended","source":"Kalat Biological Psychology 14e uploaded PDF + existing source-grounded topic map","totalWords":194},"studyDepth":"guided_deep"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h08","title":"Biochemical Mechanisms","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m12-3-h07","printedPage":411,"pdfPage":429,"explanation":"Synaptic strengthening depends on molecular events that detect activity and change receptor function or synaptic structure. The details vary with the synapse and form of plasticity.","paragraphIndex":20021,"bullets":[{"label":"Receptor roles","explanation":"For many hippocampal synapses, NMDA receptor activation permits calcium entry under suitable electrical conditions; calcium-dependent pathways alter AMPA receptor activity.","paragraphIndex":20022},{"label":"Stability","explanation":"Short-term adjustments can occur quickly, while more lasting changes may require altered gene expression, protein production and restructuring of synapses.","paragraphIndex":20023},{"label":"Early changes","explanation":"Phosphorylation and movement or altered activity of receptors can change synaptic efficiency rapidly.","paragraphIndex":74314},{"label":"Lasting changes","explanation":"More persistent plasticity may involve new proteins and structural alterations. The precise pathway depends on the circuit, timing, and kind of learning.","paragraphIndex":74315}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Synaptic plasticity depends on cascades of intracellular reactions, not merely a single transmitter entering or leaving a synapse. Such cascades can modify proteins and sometimes gene expression.","followUpParagraphIndex":53207,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h09","title":"Improving Memory","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":413,"pdfPage":431,"explanation":"Memory improvement has no single biological switch. The book contrasts plausible methods and the difficulty of proving that a treatment benefits everyday learning.","paragraphIndex":20024,"bullets":[{"label":"Practical influences","explanation":"Sleep and appropriately spaced learning help retention by allowing reactivation and reducing interference; repetition alone is less useful without retrieval.","paragraphIndex":20025},{"label":"Evaluate claims","explanation":"Distinguish better performance on a narrow laboratory task from a reliable improvement in broad memory ability, and consider side effects when evaluating drugs or supplements.","paragraphIndex":20026},{"label":"Practical study principle","explanation":"Studying thoroughly, rehearsing later, periodically testing recall, exercising, sleeping adequately, eating well, and managing stress are the practical approaches the textbook favors over claims about a universal 'memory enhancer.'","paragraphIndex":74316},{"label":"Evaluate claims","explanation":"A treatment that improves one laboratory measure does not automatically improve everyday memory or long-term understanding. Check the study design and outcome measured.","paragraphIndex":74317}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Attempts to improve memory must distinguish real learning benefits from changes in alertness, motivation, or test performance. Evidence varies across proposed methods.","followUpParagraphIndex":53208,"depth":"comprehensive_masters_with_expanded_explanations","studyDepth":"standard_existing"},{"headingId":"bp14-m12-3-h10","title":"In Closing: The Physiology of Memory","level":1,"parentId":null,"printedPage":414,"pdfPage":432,"explanation":"The best-supported cellular lesson is that experience can modify synaptic communication, but behavioral learning requires circuits, not isolated molecules.","paragraphIndex":20027,"bullets":[{"label":"Levels of explanation","explanation":"Neurotransmitter release and receptor changes explain local plasticity; networks determine which memories and skills emerge from it.","paragraphIndex":20028},{"label":"Essential link","explanation":"A strong account connects the manipulation of a synapse to a measurable behavioral difference, as seen in simple learning systems and studied in vertebrates.","paragraphIndex":20029},{"label":"Scale connection","explanation":"A synaptic change can alter a circuit; a change in circuit function can alter how an organism learns or responds.","paragraphIndex":74318},{"label":"Avoid overgeneralization","explanation":"Habituation, sensitization, LTP, and human episodic memory should be compared, not collapsed into one identical process.","paragraphIndex":74319}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Cellular studies describe processes capable of supporting memory, while behavioral studies show when those changes actually matter. Be careful not to equate brain size alone with intelligence or to confuse correlation with explanation."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-4-study-1","text":"What intelligence scores represent"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Intelligence research examines performance across many cognitive tasks. Scores often correlate positively, suggesting that some abilities are shared across tasks, while additional specific skills contribute to individual differences. The statistical factor sometimes called general intelligence summarizes a pattern of test performance; it is not a physical substance that researchers have located in one part of the brain. A careful explanation distinguishes the measurement model from the biological processes that might influence it."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-4-study-2","text":"Genetics and experience"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Research on relatives and adoption provides information about genetic contributions to variation in intelligence-test performance. Such studies require the same caution as any heritability finding: a population estimate does not determine an individual's capacity or make educational and environmental influences irrelevant. Prenatal conditions, health, learning opportunities, and many other factors can affect cognitive development. Observed group differences cannot be casually attributed to a single biological cause."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-4-study-3","text":"Brain size is only a partial clue"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brains differ across species and among individuals, but absolute brain size is a poor stand-alone predictor of cognitive abilities. The organization of neural circuits, patterns of connectivity, body size, and the specific capacities required by an environment matter. Correlations between some anatomical measures and performance do not mean that increasing the size of a brain region directly increases intelligence. Comparative studies are especially challenging because species excel at different tasks."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-4-study-4","text":"An integrated view"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding intelligence biologically requires connecting development, neural processing, learning, and the demands of measurement. The chapter emphasizes important evidence without providing a simple 'intelligence center.' In revision, separate definitions of the construct, ways it is measured, estimates of genetic influence, and hypotheses about neural mechanisms. Each is a distinct scientific question."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-4-h01","text":"Genetics and Intelligence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As with almost any psychological variable, variations in intelligence reflect contributions from both genetic and environmental influences.","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Evidence for a genetic effect includes the observation that monozygotic twins resemble each other more strongly than do dizygotic twins on tests of overall intelligence, specific cognitive abilities, and brain volume .","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Heritability increases as people grow older, presumably because high-performing people gravitate toward educational opportunities and activities that facilitate and magnify their genetic predispositions (Haworth et al., 2010;","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Also, as adopted children grow older, the correlation of their test scores with their adoptive relatives decreases somewhat, while the correlation with their biological parents increases .","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many genes known to be important for intelligence are described as “intolerant of variation” .","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For people within the normal range of intelligence, researchers have identified more than a thousand gene variations with small but measurable correlations with intelligence .","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If a gene correlates with intellectual function, we need research to find out why.","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-4-h02","text":"Brain Size and Intelligence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People sometimes use the term brainy to mean intelligent.","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We assume that bigger brains are better, but it is not that simple.","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the 1800s and early 1900s, members of several societies of successful and famous men—yes, all men— agreed to donate their brains after death for research into the causes of their success.","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The brains of the eminent people varied considerably, as did those of less eminent people .","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Becoming eminent depends on opportunity, luck, effort, and so much else.","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-4-h03","text":"Comparing Species"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, this trend does not hold when we compare species from separate families.","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, brain-to-body ratio has limitations also: Chihuahuas have the highest brain-to-body ratio of all dog breeds, not because they were bred for intelligence but because they were bred for small bodies .","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, humans do lead in one aspect, by a considerable margin: total number of neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although marmosets have a greater brain-to-body ratio than humans, marmosets’ bodies are smaller, and therefore they have fewer neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In most animal families, the species with larger brains also have larger neurons, so that the ones with larger brains have only moderately larger numbers of neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In primates, however, the species with larger brains have the same size neurons as those with smaller brains.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Thus, total number of neurons may be a reasonable correlate of intelligence (to the extent that we regard intelligence as a reasonable concept when comparing species).","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Further support comes from the observation that birds in the crow and parrot families, which have demonstrated impressive problem-solving skills , have as many neurons as a small monkey, because crows’ and parrots’ neurons are so tightly packed .","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-4-h04","text":"Human Data"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For many years, studies of human brain size and intelligence found correlations near zero.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A low correlation between variables can mean that they are unrelated, but it can also mean that one or both variables were measured poorly.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The best way to conduct a study is to compare people within a family.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"With that design, researchers found a correlation of 0.18 with one population sample and 0.19 with another .","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Intelligence scores correlate with total brain volume, surface area of the cortex, several white-matter tracts, and","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, although the correlations are interesting, they are far too low to make useful predictions about an individual .","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One possibility is that females may have smaller neurons, and therefore the same number of neurons and synapses packed into a smaller volume.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"On average, some brain areas form a larger percentage of the male brain and others form a larger percentage of the female brain .","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The apparent link between intelligence and brain size or the number of neurons can take us only so far.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A good understanding of brain processes or psychological processes requires analysis of the more detailed ways in which each brain area contributes to specific aspects of behavior and experience.","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-4-h05","text":"Brain Evolution"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Except for the specializations related to language, human brains are organized the same way as those of other mammals.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We have the same types of neurons, the same neurotransmitters, the same types of synapses, approximately the same ratio of neurons to glia cells, and so forth .","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A few other genetic changes altered synaptic transmission in a few brain areas .","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The human brain constitutes only 2 percent of the body’s mass, but it consumes 20 percent of its fuel.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When researchers selectively bred guppies (small fish) for larger brains, they found that these guppies had less energy available for other organs, including the reproductive system, and the guppies produced fewer than average offspring .","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For our remote ancestors to evolve such large brains, they needed to get a great deal of nutrition, but they also needed to reduce the energy spent on other functions.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-4-h06","text":"In Closing: Why Are We So Intelligent?"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We cook our food, we share food, we cooperate for raising children, and we have big brains.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The humans of today are the product of an amazing and very special evolutionary history.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At some point in our early evolutionary history, our ancestors learned to cook their food, making it easier to digest.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Also, they hunted in groups, bringing back more food than one person alone could find, and they learned to catch fish and harvest shellfish, rich in nutrition.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hunting in groups and making tools for weapons made it possible to get food without such big muscles.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Compared to most species, people bear fewer offspring over a lifetime but devote enough care to increase the probability of survival.","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"Monozygotic twins resemble each other even if they are reared separately.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h01","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435},{"type":"bullet","text":"Still, much else can modify intelligence, including effects of health, diet, education, and exposure to air pollution.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h01","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435},{"type":"bullet","text":"That is, they are the same in almost everyone, and mutations in them lead to intellectual disability.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h01","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, any gene that is more common in southeast Asia than in other parts of the world would correlate with eating more rice.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h01","sourcePrintedPage":417,"sourcePdfPage":435},{"type":"bullet","text":"Long ago, Bernhard Rensch (1964) demonstrated that within a family of animals, the larger species, which have larger brains, learn faster and remember better than smaller species.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h03","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436},{"type":"bullet","text":"Larger rodents do better than smaller rodents, and larger species in the chicken family do better than smaller ones.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h03","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436},{"type":"bullet","text":"Early studies measured skull size to estimate brain size, but skull size and brain size do not match well.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h04","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437},{"type":"bullet","text":"(Some people are thick skulled!) Today, measurements based on MRI find a low positive correlation between brain size and IQ score.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h04","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you want to identify smart people, attend to their actions, not their brain measurements, just as you would identify good athletes by their performance and not their muscle size.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h04","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437},{"type":"bullet","text":"A theoretical problem arises: Men on average have about 10 percent larger brains than women but equal IQ scores.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h04","sourcePrintedPage":419,"sourcePdfPage":437},{"type":"bullet","text":"Just a few genetic differences between humans and other primates are enough to cause more rapid and more prolonged production of neurons during embryological development, leading to a larger cerebral cortex and a larger number of neurons.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h05","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438},{"type":"bullet","text":"Expressing one of those genes in a marmoset monkey caused expansion of the cortex and extra folds in the surface.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h05","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438},{"type":"bullet","text":"Humans are like other mammals in many ways, but we are also unusual.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h06","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438},{"type":"bullet","text":"The big brains were important for cooking, sharing, and raising children.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h06","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438},{"type":"bullet","text":"Furthermore, humans differ from chimpanzees in two genes responsible for glucose transport: We have more of the protein that transports glucose into the brain, and less of the protein that transports it into the muscles.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h06","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438},{"type":"bullet","text":"Persisting family groups and food sharing within a community made it easier to raise an infant.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h06","sourcePrintedPage":420,"sourcePdfPage":438},{"type":"bullet","text":"However, this trend does not hold when we compare species from separate families.","headingId":"bp14-m12-4-h02","sourcePrintedPage":418,"sourcePdfPage":436},{"type":"bullet","text":"For many years, studies of human brain size and intelligence found correlations near
